stimulus.title: A green laser pointer
stimulus.html: A green laser pointer emits light with a wavelength of 532 nm. Inside it, an infrared laser at 1064 nm produces the light that is converted to green.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Calculate the frequency of the green light.

rubric.point: ν = c/λ with λ in meters: 5.64 × 10¹⁴ s⁻¹.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Calculate the energy of one photon of the green light, in joules.

rubric.point: E = hν = 3.73 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, consistent with part (a).

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Calculate the energy of one mole of these photons, in kJ/mol.

rubric.point: Multiplies by Avogadro's number and converts to kJ: 225 kJ/mol.

parts.sample: 3.7340 × 10⁻¹⁹ J × 6.022 × 10²³ mol⁻¹ = 2.2486 × 10⁵ J/mol = 224.9 kJ/mol, which is 225 kJ/mol.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: A dye needs 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J to promote an electron to an excited state. A student says the 1064 nm infrared beam will excite the dye if it is made bright enough. Explain why the student is incorrect.

rubric.point: Each 1064 nm photon carries about 1.87 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, less than the 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J gap; a transition needs one photon of matching energy, and brightness adds photons, not energy per photon.
accept: energy per photon is too small
brightness changes the number of photons only

parts.sample: Each 1064 nm photon has E = hc/λ = 1.87 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, less than the 3.0 × 10⁻¹⁹ J needed. An electron absorbs one photon at a time, so the photon itself must match the gap. A brighter beam has more photons, but each still has too little energy.
